name: Pedro Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead carpenter at a building co-op, which means the workers own the firm, and we put up timber-frame houses. Half my week is in our workshop, where the wall panels get cut and nailed, and half is on site, standing the panels up with the crane and fixing the roof. First thing every morning I'm on my phone asking an AI assistant to check the day's cutting list against the drawings. The part I love is the day a house goes from a bare slab to a roof in four days. The part that wears me out is the rain, always the rain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: An AI assistant checking cutting lists isn't what most people picture on a building site. How did you start using it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My daughter Lucía showed me, about three years ago, because I was moaning about a panel we'd cut wrong. I tried it that night with a photo of the drawing and it found a mistake in a window opening that I'd missed. Now I use it for everything, ordering timber, writing up the safety plan, even arguing with the council's planning department. The younger lads think it's funny that the oldest man on site is the one with the gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly. I'd tell people it's still a great tool for the boring stuff, and they should use it. Online I'd probably post a photo of a cutting list it caught and say, see, it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing really changes. I work till sixty-five or so, the co-op keeps going, I hand over to younger ones. It's a comfortable picture, a bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on using the tools I use, and I'd run a little lunchtime session for the crew on how to get the most out of them, because most of them only use it for the football scores. I'd keep putting about a hundred and fifty a month away, same as now. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little bit of "oh well". I was curious where it would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointed is an unusual word to hear about this. Why disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what it does for me, and I hoped it would take the drudgery out of the whole trade. There's a lot of standing in the rain waiting for a delivery that a smarter system could plan away. If it stalls, we keep the drudgery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you most want at that lunchtime session?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hamid, he's forty-five and he's the best panel man we have, but he does all his sums on a scrap of plasterboard. He's not against it, he just thinks it's not for him. If I can get Hamid using it, everyone follows.

S0.say: He's a bit disappointed, but it's still a great tool for the boring stuff and people should use it. Online he'd post a photo of a cutting list it caught.
S0.think: Nothing really changes: he works until about sixty-five, the co-op carries on and he hands over to younger ones. It's comfortable but a bit flat.
S0.do: Keeps using his current tools and runs lunchtime sessions to teach the crew how to use them better. Keeps saving about a hundred and fifty a month, as now.
S0.feel: Calm, with a mild "oh well" because he was curious where it would go.
S0.quote: There's a lot of standing in the rain waiting for a delivery that a smarter system could plan away. If it stalls, we keep the drudgery.
S0.fieldNote: Unusually for his age and trade, he's mildly let down by the plateau because he hoped AI would cut the drudgery. He's the crew's informal teacher on the tools. He wants to win over Hamid, the skilled panel man who does sums on plasterboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to do it right. In a co-op, if a machine does more of the work, we all own the machine, so we all get the benefit, shorter weeks maybe. I'd be saying that to anyone who'd listen, and I'd write it up for our members' newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm excited. Our workshop could take a lot more automation, a robot nailing the panels while the people do the tricky bits. The worry is the big builders do it first and undercut us on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a proposal to the co-op meeting in the first few months to buy an automated nailing bridge for the workshop, the kind that runs over the panel on a frame. I'd go on the supplier's training course myself, and take Hamid. I'd push for us to use the time it saves for a four-day week rather than fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A little edge of worry about the big firms beating us to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a robot nailing panels. What would happen to the people who do that now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are three of us on nailing. The idea is they move to the fiddly jobs, the windows, the insulation, quality checks, and we use the extra speed to build more houses. If we vote it in, nobody gets let go, that's a rule we'd write into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op members vote it down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost a vote and I'd try again next year with better numbers. That's how it works when the workers own it. I'd rather lose a vote among friends than have a boss decide for us.

S1.say: This is the chance to do it right: in a co-op the workers own the machines, so everyone shares the benefit, maybe as shorter weeks. He'd write it up for the members' newsletter.
S1.think: He's privately excited that the workshop could take much more automation. His worry is that the big builders automate first and undercut the co-op on price.
S1.do: Proposes buying an automated nailing bridge at a co-op meeting within months and attends the supplier's training with a colleague. Pushes for the saved time to become a four-day week, with a rule that nobody is let go.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a small edge of worry about big firms getting there first.
S1.quote: I'd rather lose a vote among friends than have a boss decide for us.
S1.fieldNote: His progressive outlook and his appetite for technology fit together through worker ownership: automation is fine if the workers own the machines. He'd move first and propose specific kit. His one worry is competition from bigger firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the machines aren't the enemy, but the way it's happening is a disaster. If a handful of companies own all the robots, everyone else is just waiting for scraps. I'd be out marching for public ownership of some of this, and online every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I could probably adapt, I'd be the one running the robots. But our co-op has a few months of cash and so do I, and if the big firms flood the market with robot-built houses at half the price, we could go under in a year. And I'm sixty in 2028, so if that happens it's late to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd go to the co-op and say we need to automate now, take a loan if we must, because standing still is death. I'd build up my own savings fast, cut the eating out, sell the second van we barely use. And I'd be at every protest and meeting pushing for a tax on robot owners and a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and angry. Not about the robots, about who'll own them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take a loan to automate at the same time as cutting back yourself. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, a bit. But the co-op's risk and my risk are different things. For the co-op, the worst move is doing nothing. For my own house, the worst move is being caught with no money, so I'd be careful at home and bold at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucía, who showed you the AI in the first place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's tough, because she's a software tester, and that's exactly what it would eat first. I'd tell her she's got the skills to be on the side that builds it and directs it, not the side it replaces. And I'd tell her to come to the march with me.

S2.say: The machines aren't the enemy, but the way it's happening is a disaster if a handful of companies own all the robots. He'd march for public ownership and post every night.
S2.think: He could adapt personally, but the co-op and he each have only a few months of cash, and robot-built houses at half price could sink the co-op within a year. At sixty, starting again would be hard.
S2.do: Urges the co-op to automate immediately, borrowing if needed. Cuts eating out and sells the spare van to build savings, and campaigns at protests for a tax on robot owners and a basic income.
S2.feel: Anxious and angry, not at the robots but at who will own them.
S2.quote: For my own house, the worst move is being caught with no money, so I'd be careful at home and bold at work.
S2.fieldNote: He separates the co-op's risk from his household's: bold at work, careful at home. The threat he names is not AI itself but concentrated ownership and price competition. When asked about the apparent contradiction he answered thoughtfully rather than defensively.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make sure the gains are shared, if we get organised now. I'd be talking about co-ops a lot, because I think it's the answer. People would get sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for us. It gives the co-op time to automate the workshop properly and to learn what robots can do on site. For me, I'd be sixty-three and I could be the person who runs and fixes the machines until I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the co-op to put money aside each year for new kit, maybe ten percent of our surplus. I'd do a proper course on site robotics in the first year, evenings if I have to. And I'd help two or three other building co-ops in the region plan the same, because together we can buy kit cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. The kind of nervous where you've got too much to do to dwell on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a course on site robotics actually look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know yet, and that's honest. Probably the supplier's courses plus something at the technical college, programming the machines, safety, maintenance. I'd be the oldest in the class by thirty years and I'd love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said helping other co-ops. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a roofing co-op across town and a joinery one near the old docks. We already share a crane now and then. If the three of us bought a robot together and rotated it, none of us would have to bet the farm.

S3.say: Five years is enough to make sure the gains are shared if people get organised now. He'd talk about co-ops so much people would get sick of him.
S3.think: Five years is good for the co-op: time to automate the workshop and learn what site robots can do. At sixty-three he could run and maintain the machines until he retires.
S3.do: Pushes the co-op to set aside about ten percent of its surplus each year for new kit and takes a site robotics course in the first year. Helps two other local co-ops plan to share and buy kit together.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, too occupied to dwell on it.
S3.quote: I'd be the oldest in the class by thirty years and I'd love it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a project. He'd retrain at sixty-three without hesitation and openly admits he doesn't know what the course would involve. His instinct is to build alliances, sharing kit between co-ops so none of them bets everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to make this the best thing that ever happened to working people, so let's not waste it. Shorter weeks, shared ownership, good pensions. I'd be optimistic out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm retired, sixty-eight, probably pottering in the co-op workshop as a volunteer. I'd love to see a robot stand up a house. The worry is what's left for Mateo and Lucía's generation if we get it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help the co-op build a ten-year plan, step by step, which kit when, who retrains for what. I'd keep using the AI tools every day and keep teaching the crew. I'd retire on schedule at sixty-five and hand over properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit hopeful. This is the version where we get to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo, who's a chef?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will still want to eat food made by a person who cares, at least in some places, the way people still buy a handmade table. But I'd tell him to think about owning his own place one day, or a share of one. Owning is safer than working for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to ownership. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father worked thirty years in a sawmill and got a handshake when it closed. When I joined the co-op at forty I promised myself I'd never be in that position. It's the same with robots, the question is always, whose are they.

S4.say: There's a decade to make this the best thing that ever happened to working people, so it mustn't be wasted. He'd argue for shorter weeks, shared ownership and good pensions.
S4.think: By 2036 he'll be retired and would love to see a robot stand up a house. His worry is what's left for his children's generation if it goes wrong.
S4.do: Helps the co-op draw up a ten-year plan for kit and retraining. Keeps using and teaching AI tools daily and retires on schedule at sixty-five with a proper handover.
S4.feel: Calm and a little hopeful; this is the version where they get to steer.
S4.quote: My father worked thirty years in a sawmill and got a handshake when it closed.
S4.fieldNote: The decade-long picture is the one he welcomes, because it allows planning. His focus on ownership traces directly to his father being let go from a sawmill. He's the only person so far who'd enjoy watching robots do his old job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time for small firms like ours to adapt and the big money gets there first. What would help is cheap loans for co-ops and small builders to buy the machines, and a tax on robot owners that pays for a basic income. Give the robots to the workers, basically.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want robots on my site. I would. I just want them to be ours.

headlineQuote: It's the same with robots, the question is always, whose are they.
portrait: Pedro is a fifty-eight-year-old lead carpenter at a worker-owned timber-frame building co-op who uses AI tools every day, first shown them by his daughter. He's the rare veteran who is disappointed by the plateau and excited by steady change, which he'd use to propose automating the co-op's workshop with no lay-offs. AGI in two years makes him anxious because the co-op and he both have only a few months of cash and big firms could undercut them. With five or ten years, he'd retrain in site robotics and plan kit-sharing with other co-ops. Everything he says comes back to ownership, rooted in his father's sawmill closure.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because small firms like his co-op would have no time to adapt before big companies with robots undercut them.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for co-ops and small builders to buy the machines, and a tax on robot owners that funds a basic income.
